notes: Replevin/lien dispute over a third party's sewing machine detained by a boarding-house keeper for an unpaid board bill; the boarder/guest/innkeeper distinctions discussed are background to the lien-priority holding, not to the legality or regulation of letting rooms itself. Duplicate report of Barnett v. Walker (also 39 Misc. 323): lien-priority dispute over a third party's sewing machine detained by a boarding-house keeper, not a dispute over the legality or regulation of letting rooms.

Dispute over an innkeeper's common-law lien on a piano owned by a third-party conditional vendor, left at defendant's hotel by a guest (later a one-year apartment tenant); addresses scope/constitutionality of the innkeeper's lien over third-party property, not the legality or regulation of letting/boarding. Guest occupied roughly Aug. 1898-Mar. 1899, then leased apartment for a year, occupied to June 1899.

court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
holding_summary: A widow occupying only one or two of sixteen rooms in a leased house, whose sole livelihood was letting the remaining rooms to boarders/roomers, was held still to occupy the premises 'for dwelling purposes' under the 1920 emergency rent-suspension statute, because letting rooms to lodgers is merely incidental to the tenant's own occupation of the house as her home. The landlord's summary proceeding to recover possession after the tenancy's expiration was accordingly barred by the statute and properly dismissed.

court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
holding_summary: In a summary non-payment proceeding against the tenant of a house leased as 'a residence and rooming house,' the court held that the parts of the premises let to roomers and table boarders were used for business rather than dwelling purposes, so the landlord was entitled to recover possession of those parts, while the trial court must separately fix a reasonable rent only for the portion the tenant actually occupied as his own dwelling. The final order fixing rent for the entire premises was reversed and a new trial ordered.

quotes.text: The tenant with his wife and daughter occupies the front parlor and kitchen; the front basement contains six tables set for table boarders and all the rest of the house is occupied by roomers.

it would seem to follow that the landlord on non-payment of the rents of such a house is entitled to the possession of those parts of the premises occupied by roomers, and it would be the duty of the trial court to fix a reasonable rental for so much of the house used as a dwelling by the tenant.

notes: Characterization marked 'other' because the court's holding bifurcates the premises into a protected dwelling portion and an unprotected business (roomer/table-boarder) portion rather than applying a single lease/license/lodging label. Duration of individual roomers' stays not specified.

court: New York City Municipal Court, First District
notes: Replevin action addressing whether a boarding-house keeper's statutory lien attaches to a third party's furniture brought onto the premises by a boarder who 'remained for several weeks'; concerns lien priority against the true owner under the constitution, not the legality of the boarding arrangement itself.

Liquor Tax Law proceeding over whether premises were continuously occupied as a 'hotel' to preserve a liquor-tax certificate exemption; the hotel/boarding-house distinction (guest vs. boarder paying by the week) is used only to determine liquor-license eligibility, not the legality or regulation of letting rooms/dwellings for pay.

Replevin action over a hotel/apartment company's claimed lien on a tenant's wife's furniture; turns on whether the husband under a formal one-year lease was a 'tenant' (no lien) rather than a 'lodger' for lien-law purposes -- a lien-priority classification question, not a dispute over the legality of letting or boarding.

court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Department
holding_summary: A house occupied under a restrictive covenant limiting use to 'one private dwelling house' was rented, by oral arrangement, to three unrelated families who pooled rent and household/food expenses under the management of one of them; the court held this violated the covenant, reasoning that the arrangement's status and service were similar to a boarding-house keeper's, and that occupancy by multiple unrelated families destroys the singleness and privacy of a private dwelling. The order denying an injunction was reversed and the injunction granted.

court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
notes: Determines whether a 140-room apartment building with 15 furnished transient rooms qualifies as a 'hotel' exempt from a rent-emergency statute's bill-of-particulars requirement; concerns statutory classification of a large commercial apartment-hotel enterprise, not a householder's letting of dwelling space or police-power regulation of lodging houses.

court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
holding_summary: A restrictive covenant confining lots to 'first class dwelling houses' and enumerating specific prohibited nuisance-type businesses did not bar a resident from privately taking in boarders, because boarding houses -- though as well known when the covenant was drawn as today -- were not among the uses expressly prohibited, and the house was not held out to the public, took no transients, and admitted only boarders personally known or recommended. The neighboring owner's suit to enjoin the use as a boarding house was dismissed.

quotes.text: No transient guests are received, but on the contrary, several of the guests have lived in the household of the defendant Ida M. court: Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
holding_summary: The Appellate Division majority held that a tenant who allowed a family to occupy two upper floors of his leased dwelling for about three years, paying 55% of household expenses and given a separate kitchen, bathroom, and doorbell, had in substance sublet those floors in violation of the lease's no-subletting covenant, rejecting the claim that the occupant was merely a lodger. The dissent, invoking the settled rule that letting rooms to lodgers is not a breach of a covenant against under-letting, would have found no violation.

holding_summary: A boarding-house keeper sued a former boarder for breach of an entire contract to pay $100 a month for a room and board for himself and his wife through a fixed period; the Appellate Term upheld a jury verdict for the boarding-house keeper, finding the entire character of the contract corroborated by a disinterested witness and that she was not obligated to relet the room where the departing boarder said he would arrange for it himself. The judgment was affirmed as not excessive.

quotes.text: The plaintiff, a boarding house keeper, sued for the defendant’s breach of an entire contract whereby he agreed to pay $100 a month for a room and board for himself and his wife during a period ending July 9, 1902.
As to the entire character of the contract, the plaintiff’s testimony was corroborated by a disinterested witness, and we find no reason for disturbing the jury’s conclusion upon the facts.

notes: Contract enforcement dispute between a commercial boarding-house keeper and a boarder over an entire monthly room-and-board agreement; probative of courts enforcing boarding arrangements as ordinary contracts, though the core issue is contract/mitigation doctrine rather than legality of letting per se.

notes: Tort action for a lost gown turning on whether an apartment-hotel building (with kitchens, restaurant, weekly billing) was an 'inn' imposing common-law innkeeper strict liability, or an apartment house where plaintiff (who stayed about a week) was merely a tenant doing 'light housekeeping'; concerns innkeeper-bailee tort classification, not the legality or regulation of letting/boarding.
